content: The World Medical Association (WMA) developed the Declaration of Helsinki to establish ethical principles for guiding physicians and other participants in medical research involving human subjects. This includes research on identifiable human material or data. Physicians have a duty to promote and safeguard the health of people, dedicating their knowledge and conscience to this responsibility. Medical progress relies on research, which often involves experimentation on human subjects. However, the well-being of human subjects must always take precedence over the interests of science and society. The primary goal of medical research involving human subjects is to improve preventive, diagnostic, and therapeutic procedures, as well as to enhance understanding of disease etiology and pathogenesis. Even the most proven methods must be continuously evaluated for their effectiveness, efficiency, accessibility, and quality through research. Medical research is subject to ethical standards that respect all human beings and protect their health and rights. Vulnerable populations require special protection, including those who are economically or medically disadvantaged, those unable to give or refuse consent, those at risk of coercion, and those who will not personally benefit from the research. Researchers must also consider the ethical, legal, and regulatory requirements of their country and applicable international standards, ensuring that no national regulations reduce the protections outlined in the Declaration. Physicians conducting medical research must protect the life, health, privacy, and dignity of human subjects. Research must adhere to accepted scientific principles, be based on thorough knowledge of the scientific literature, and include adequate laboratory and, where appropriate, animal experimentation. Research protocols must be clearly formulated and submitted for review and approval by an independent ethical review committee, which has the authority to monitor ongoing trials. Researchers are obligated to provide monitoring information, including serious adverse events, and disclose funding sources, institutional affiliations, potential conflicts of interest, and subject incentives. Informed consent is a cornerstone of ethical research. Subjects must be adequately informed about the aims, methods, funding sources, potential conflicts of interest, anticipated benefits, risks, and discomforts of the study. They must also be informed of their right to abstain from participation or withdraw consent at any time without reprisal. Consent should be obtained in writing whenever possible, and if not, it must be formally documented and witnessed. Special care must be taken when obtaining consent from individuals in dependent relationships with the physician or those who may consent under duress. In such cases, consent should be obtained by an independent, well-informed physician not involved in the investigation. For legally incompetent individuals, such as minors or those unable to give consent due to physical or mental incapacity, informed consent must be obtained from a legally authorized representative. These groups should only be included in research if it is necessary to promote the health of the population they represent and cannot be conducted on legally competent individuals. When legally incompetent individuals can provide assent, their assent must be obtained in addition to the consent of their legal representative. Research involving individuals unable to provide consent, including proxy or advance consent, should only be conducted if their condition is a necessary characteristic of the research population. The reasons for involving such subjects must be stated in the protocol and approved by the review committee. Consent to remain in the research should be obtained as soon as possible from the individual or their legal representative. Both authors and publishers have ethical obligations to ensure the accuracy of research results. Negative and positive results should be published or made publicly available, with funding sources, institutional affiliations, and potential conflicts of interest disclosed. Reports of research not adhering to the principles of the Declaration should not be accepted for publication. Physicians may combine medical research with medical care only if the research is justified by its potential preventive, diagnostic, or therapeutic value. Additional standards apply to protect patients who are also research subjects. The benefits, risks, burdens, and effectiveness of new methods should be tested against the best current methods. Placebo-controlled trials are acceptable only in the absence of proven therapy or under specific, scientifically justified circumstances. At the conclusion of a study, all patients involved should have access to the best proven methods identified by the research. Physicians must inform patients about which aspects of their care are related to research, and a patient’s refusal to participate must not interfere with the patient-physician relationship. In cases where proven methods are unavailable or ineffective, physicians may use unproven or new methods with informed consent if they offer hope of saving life, restoring health, or alleviating suffering. These measures should ideally be part of research designed to evaluate their safety and efficacy, with new information recorded and published where appropriate. All relevant guidelines of the Declaration must be followed.
